item.title: No forced religious activities or fundraising contributions in schools – Voresara
item.description: Students and teachers should not be forced to participate in religious activities that go against their beliefs, while schools will be required to properly account for money collected from parents under the Education Act 2026. Principal Education Officer Amini Voresara highlighted these requirements during the Ministry of Representatives' public consultation at the Lami Parish Catholic Hall.
item.content:encoded:
Students and teachers should not be forced to participate in religious activities that go against their beliefs, while schools will be required to properly account for money collected from parents under the Education Act 2026.

Principal Education Officer Amini Voresara highlighted these requirements during the Ministry of Representatives' public consultation at the Lami Parish Catholic Hall.

Voresara says schools must respect the religious beliefs of all students and teachers, regardless of the school's religious affiliation.

He says even in faith-based schools, students and teachers who follow a different religion should not be required to participate in religious activities against their beliefs.

Voresara cites Catholic schools as an example, saying teachers who are not Catholic should not be forced to attend religious activities against their wishes.

He says the same principle applies to students from different religious backgrounds .

Voresara stresses that schools must respect individual beliefs and ensure everyone is treated fairly.

Meanwhile, the Principal Education Officer says schools will also be required to properly account for money collected from parents, including building and sports levies.

He says school management teams and heads of schools must ensure that all money collected is properly recorded and used for its intended purpose.

Voresara says schools cannot introduce levies without approval, as requests for building and sports levies must go through the Permanent Secretary for Education.

He says money collected from parents for a building project must be used for that project and cannot be diverted to social activities or other purposes.

Voresara stresses that school management teams and heads of schools will be held accountable if funds are misused.

He says all schools, including boarding schools, will also be required to prepare annual financial reports and submit them to the Ministry of Education.

Voresara says concerns have been raised about schools collecting money from parents without proper approval or accountability.

He says some schools have collected funds several times a year without obtaining the necessary approval.

The Principal Education Officer also stresses that parents and guardians cannot be forced to contribute to school fundraising activities.

He says all fundraising contributions must be voluntary, even when fundraising activities have been approved.

Voresara adds that parents who choose not to contribute must not be treated unfairly.

He says the new requirements aim to protect individual rights, strengthen financial accountability and ensure schools treat students, teachers and parents fairly.

The Education Act 2026 is expected to come into effect on 1 January 2027.

item.title: Mahesh Syndicate honours late founder with Special Legacy Diwali Sale
item.description: This Diwali, Mahesh Syndicate launches The Special Legacy Diwali Sale as the company honours its late founder, Mahesh Kumar, who played a pivotal role in introducing a wide variety of fireworks to Fiji since the 1970s. Mahesh Syndicate Director Vinay Kumar says this year's special diwali legacy sale is particularly emotional for the company, following the passing of its founder three months ago.
item.content:encoded:
This Diwali, Mahesh Syndicate launches The Special Legacy Diwali Sale as the company honours its late founder, Mahesh Kumar, who played a pivotal role in introducing a wide variety of fireworks to Fiji since the 1970s.

Mahesh Syndicate Director Vinay Kumar says this year's special diwali legacy sale is particularly emotional for the company, following the passing of its founder three months ago.

Kumar says Mahesh Kumar was instrumental in shaping Fiji's fireworks industry, introducing several types of fireworks that became popular among Fijians and helped establish large-scale commercial fireworks sales in the country.

He says some of the fireworks introduced by the late founder, including the Single Shot Double Bang, Single Shot Thunder King and Egg Cracker, remain popular today.

Kumar says the company is proud to honour his contribution and continue the legacy he established over the past five decades.

Speaking about the significance of Diwali, Kumar says the festival represents the triumph of good over evil and is a time for reflection, spreading kindness and strengthening relationships with those around us.

He says Diwali has grown in significance around the world, with people from different communities and backgrounds joining in the celebrations.

Meanwhile, he says this year has been particularly challenging for the fireworks importation industry, with new compliance requirements in Fiji, restrictions in China and increased freight costs affecting the availability and prices of fireworks.

Kumar says following explosions at fireworks manufacturing facilities in China in early May, additional restrictions and certification requirements were introduced, creating further challenges for importers.

He says freight costs for dangerous goods have also increased by around 30 to 35 percent.

Kumar says fireworks importation in Fiji is now subject to increased regulation, with the Ministry of Defence also involved alongside the Ministry of Mineral Resources.

He says these additional compliance requirements have increased the overall cost of importing fireworks, with some products also unable to receive the necessary certification in time for this year's sales.

Kumar says this has resulted in fewer fireworks being available in the Fijian market, with only a handful of companies managing to import supplies this year.

He says sales have remained relatively stagnant, with the company expecting more customers in the final days leading up to Diwali as families usually prioritise their grocery shopping and traditional outfits before purchasing fireworks.

Kumar says Mahesh Syndicate has managed to bring in around 40 to 45 varieties of fireworks this year, despite the challenges adding the range includes cakes, fountains, sparklers, pop-ups and small crackers.

Mahesh Syndicate Operations Manager Nishant Kumar also reflects on growing up with fireworks from Mahesh Syndicate, saying his family has been purchasing from the company since his grandfather's generation.

Kumar says the tradition has continued through his parents, siblings and cousins, and he has also introduced his friends to the fireworks sold by the company.

He says he has personally enjoyed fireworks from Mahesh Syndicate for the past 20 years and hopes to continue that tradition.

Kumar is also reminding the public to follow the permitted fireworks hours, with fireworks allowed between 5pm and 10pm on most days.

He says an exception has been made for Diwali on Sunday, 8th November, allowing fireworks to be used between 5pm and midnight.

The Director and Operations Manager of Mahesh Syndicate have also wished all safe and happy Diwali.
